'''vasoconstrictor''' (vas″ọ̄-kon-strik′tọr), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [< L. ''vas'', vessel, + E. ''constrictor.''] '''I.''' ''a.'' Serving to constrict vessels when stimulated, as certain nerves: opposed to ''vasodilator''. Both are included under ''vasomotor''.

'''II.''' ''n.'' That which causes contraction of the blood-vessels: applied to nerves and to certain drugs.

'''vasodentinal''' (vas-ō-den′ti-nạl), ''a.'' [< ''vasodentine'' + ''-al.''] Pertaining to or having the character of vasodentine.

'''vasodentine''' (vas-ọ̄-den′tin), ''n.'' [< L. ''vas'', a vessel, + ''den(t-)s'', = E. ''tooth'', + ''-ine''<sup>2</sup>.] A vascular form of dentine in which blood circulates; dentine whose capillaries are large enough for the passage of red blood-disks. Compare ''osteodentine'' and ''vitriodentine''.

'''vasodilator''' (vas″ọ̄-di-lā′tor), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [< L. ''vas'', vessel, + E. ''dilator.''] '''I.''' ''a.'' Serving to dilate or relax blood-vessels when stimulated, as a nerve. See ''vasomotor''.

'''II.''' ''n.'' That which causes dilatation of the blood-vessels: applied to nerves and certain drugs.

'''vasoformative''' (vas-ō-fôr′ma-tiv), ''a.'' [< L. ''vas'', vessel, + E. ''formative.''] Forming or building up vessels, usually blood-vessels; vasifactive.

'''vasoganglion''' (vas-ọ̄-gang′gli-ọn), ''n.''; pl. ''vasoganglia'' (-ä). [< L. ''vas'', vessel, + E. ''ganglion.''] A network or knot of vessels; a vascular rete.

'''vaso-inhibitory''' (vas″ọ̄-in-hib′i-tō-ri), ''a.'' [< L. ''vas'', vessel, + E. ''inhibitory.''] Relating to the

'''vasomotion''' (vas-ō-mō′shọn), ''n.'' [< L. ''vas'', vessel, + E. ''motion''.] Increase or diminution of the caliber of a vessel, usually a blood-vessel.

'''vasomotor''' (vas-ọ̄-mō′tọr), ''a.'' [< L. ''vas'', vessel, + E. ''motor''.] Serving to regulate the tension of blood-vessels, as nerves; vasomotorial, whether vasoconstrictor or vasodilator. Compare ''inhibition'', 3. Also ''vasculomotor''.—'''Vasomotor center.''' {{smaller|Same as ''vascular center''. See ''vascular''.}}—'''Vasomotor coryza,''' {{smaller|a name given, in accordance with a theoretical pathology, to autumnal catarrh, or hay-fever. ''N. Y. Med. Jour.'', Sept. 3, 1887.}}—'''Vasomotor nerves,''' {{smaller|the nerves supplied to the muscular coat of the blood-vessels.}}—'''Vasomotor spasm,''' {{smaller|spasm of the middle coat of the blood-vessels.}}

'''vasomotorial''' (vas″ọ̄-mọ̄-tō′ri-ạl), ''a.'' [< ''vasomotory'' + ''-al''.] Pertaining to the vasomotor function; vasomotor.

'''vasomotoric''' (vas″ọ̄-mọ̄-tor′ik), ''a.'' [< ''vasomotor'' + ''-ic''.] Same as ''vasomotorial''.

'''vasomotory''' (vas-ọ̄-mō′tọ̄-ri), ''a.'' [< ''vasomotor'' + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.] Same as ''vasomotorial''. ''Lancet'', 1891, I. 370.

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|vase-painting|6705|vast}}</noinclude>{{smaller block|early in the fifth century {{sc|b. c.}}, and continued until vase-painting was practically abandoned, about 200 {{sc|b. c.}} It embraces the period of transition from the archaic, to which belong some of the first masters among vase-painters, and is by far the most important for study. In this style a tendency toward polychromy appears occasionally, but was not consistently worked out, except in the small but admirable class of Attic funeral lecythi. In some elaborate pieces of the fourth and third centuries, chiefly Attic, gilding is sparingly introduced. The style implies the presence of figures and of ornamental designs of every kind, very commonly in bands or zones running around the vase, in which the design appears in the natural red of the clay, details being indicated in simple black lines, and the ground being covered with solid glossy black. For examples of the red-figured decoration, see cuts under ''Greek'' and ''Poseidon''.}}

'''Vasidæ''' (vas′i-dē), ''n. pl.'' [NL., < ''Vasum'' + ''-idæ''.] A family of gastropods, named from the genus ''Vasum'': same as ''Turbinellidæ''.

'''vasifactive''' (vas-i-fak′tiv), ''a.'' [< L. ''vas'', vessel, + ''factus'', pp. of ''facere'', make (see ''fact''), + ''-ive''.] Causing a new formation of blood-vessels; angioplastic. ''Micros. Sci.'', N. S., XXX. 313.

'''vasiform''' (vas′i-fôrm), ''a.'' [< L. ''vas'', vessel, + ''forma'', form.] Having the form of a duct or other vessel; of the nature of a vas or vasculum; tubular.—'''Vasiform elements''', {{smaller|in plants, the elements, such as vessels, ducts, etc., which make up the vascular tissue.}}—'''Vasiform tissue''', {{smaller|tissue made up wholly or in part of vessels or ducts.}}

'''Vasinæ, Vasina''' (vā-sī′nē, -nä), ''n. pl.'' [NL., < ''Vasum'' + ''-inæ'', ''-ina''.] A subfamily of gastropods: same as ''Cynodontinæ''.

'''vasoconstrictive''' (vas″ọ̄-kon-strik′tiv), ''a.'' [< L. ''vas'', vessel, + E. ''constrictive''.] Same as ''vasoconstrictor''. ''W. James'', Prin. of Psychol., I. 97.

'''vasoconstrictor''' (vas″ọ̄-kon-strik′tọr), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [< L. ''vas'', vessel, + E. ''constrictor.''] '''I.''' ''a.'' Serving to constrict vessels when stimulated, as certain nerves: opposed to ''vasodilator''. Both are included under ''vasomotor''.

'''II.''' ''n.'' That which causes contraction of the blood-vessels: applied to nerves and to certain drugs.

'''vasodentinal''' (vas-ō-den′ti-nạl), ''a.'' [< ''vasodentine'' + ''-al.''] Pertaining to or having the character of vasodentine.

'''vasodentine''' (vas-ọ̄-den′tin), ''n.'' [< L. ''vas'', a vessel, + ''den(t-)s'', = E. ''tooth'', + ''-ine''<sup>2</sup>.] A vascular form of dentine in which blood circulates; dentine whose capillaries are large enough for the passage of red blood-disks. Compare ''osteodentine'' and ''vitriodentine''.

'''vasodilator''' (vas″ọ̄-di-lā′tor), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [< L. ''vas'', vessel, + E. ''dilator.''] '''I.''' ''a.'' Serving to dilate or relax blood-vessels when stimulated, as a nerve. See ''vasomotor''.

'''II.''' ''n.'' That which causes dilatation of the blood-vessels: applied to nerves and certain drugs.

'''vasoformative''' (vas-ō-fôr′ma-tiv), ''a.'' [< L. ''vas'', vessel, + E. ''formative.''] Forming or building up vessels, usually blood-vessels; vasifactive.

'''vasoganglion''' (vas-ọ̄-gang′gli-ọn), ''n.''; pl. ''vasoganglia'' (-ä). [< L. ''vas'', vessel, + E. ''ganglion.''] A network or knot of vessels; a vascular rete.

'''vaso-inhibitory''' (vas″ọ̄-in-hib′i-tō-ri), ''a.'' [< L. ''vas'', vessel, + E. ''inhibitory.''] Relating to the nerve-force causing dilatation of the blood-vessels. See ''inhibitory''.

'''vasomotion''' (vas-ō-mō′shọn), ''n.'' [< L. ''vas'', vessel, + E. ''motion''.] Increase or diminution of the caliber of a vessel, usually a blood-vessel.

'''vasomotor''' (vas-ọ̄-mō′tọr), ''a.'' [< L. ''vas'', vessel, + E. ''motor''.] Serving to regulate the tension of blood-vessels, as nerves; vasomotorial, whether vasoconstrictor or vasodilator. Compare ''inhibition'', 3. Also ''vasculomotor''.—'''Vasomotor center.''' {{smaller|Same as ''vascular center''. See ''vascular''.}}—'''Vasomotor coryza,''' {{smaller|a name given, in accordance with a theoretical pathology, to autumnal catarrh, or hay-fever. ''N. Y. Med. Jour.'', Sept. 3, 1887.}}—'''Vasomotor nerves,''' {{smaller|the nerves supplied to the muscular coat of the blood-vessels.}}—'''Vasomotor spasm,''' {{smaller|spasm of the middle coat of the blood-vessels.}}

'''vasomotorial''' (vas″ọ̄-mọ̄-tō′ri-ạl), ''a.'' [< ''vasomotory'' + ''-al''.] Pertaining to the vasomotor function; vasomotor.

'''vasomotoric''' (vas″ọ̄-mọ̄-tor′ik), ''a.'' [< ''vasomotor'' + ''-ic''.] Same as ''vasomotorial''.

'''vasomotory''' (vas-ọ̄-mō′tọ̄-ri), ''a.'' [< ''vasomotor'' + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.] Same as ''vasomotorial''. ''Lancet'', 1891, I. 370.

'''vasoperitoneal''' (vas-ọ̄-per″i-tọ̄-nē′ạl), ''a.'' [< L. ''vas'', vessel, + E. ''peritoneal''.] In echinoderms, noting the shut sac which results from the cutting off from the archenteron of a cæcal diverticulum to which the anterior part of that cavity gives rise. {{smaller|The vesicle subsequently opens on the exterior by a pore, through a diverticulum from itself, and}}

421 {{smaller block|divides later into two sections—an ambulacral sac, which lays the foundation for the whole ambulacral system of vessels, and a peritoneal sac, which gives rise to the peritoneum (whence the name).}}

'''vasosensory''' (vas-ō-sen′sō-ri), ''a.'' [< L. ''vas'', vessel, + E. ''sensory''.] Supplying sensation to the vessels: applied to sensory nerves corresponding to the vasomotor nerves.

'''vasquine''' (vas-kēn′), ''n.'' Same as ''basquine.'' ''Scott'', Abbot, II. 151.

'''vassal''' (vas′al), ''n.'' and ''a.'' [Formerly also ''vassall'', rarely ''vassaile''; < ME. ''vassal'', < OF. ''vassal'', F. ''vassal'' = Pr. ''vassal'', ''vassau'' = Cat. ''vassal'' = Sp. ''vasallo'' = Pg. It. ''vassallo'' = D. ''vassaal'' = G. Sw. ''vasall'' = Dan. ''vasal'', < ML. ''vassallus'', extended from ''vassus'', ''vasus'', a servant, < Bret. ''gwaz'', a servant, vassal, man, male, = W. ''gwas'' = Corn. ''gwas'', a youth, servant; cf. Ir. ''fas'', growing, growth, and E. ''wax''<sup>1</sup>. Hence ult. ''varlet'', ''valet'', ''vassalage'', ''vavasor''.] '''I.''' ''n.'' '''1.''' A feudatory tenant; one holding lands by the obligation to render military service or its equivalent to his superior, especially in contradistinction to ''rear vassal'' and ''vavasor''; a vassal of the first order —that is, one holding directly from the king. Compare ''great vassal'', below.
{{smaller block|The two earls . . . complained of the misrepresentations of their enemies and the oppression of their ''vassals'', and alleged that the cause of their flight was not dread of those enemies, but fear of God and the king.
{{right|''Stubbs'', Const. Hist., § 353.}}}}
{{smaller block|A ''Vassal'' or Vasseur was the holder or grantee of a feud under a prince or sovereign lord.
{{right|''W. K. Sullivan'', Introd. to O’Curry’s Anc. Irish, p. ccxxvi.}}}}

'''2.''' A subject; a dependent; a retainer; a servant; one who attends on or does the will of another.
{{smaller block|Passions ought to be her [the mind’s] ''vassals'', not her masters.
{{right|''Raleigh.''}}}}
{{smaller block|I am his fortune’s ''vassal.'' {{right|''Shak.'', A. and C., v. 2. 29.}}}}
{{smaller block|I desire not to live longer than I may be thought to be what I am, and shall ever be your faithful and obedient ''Vassal.''
{{right|''Baker'', Chronicles, p. 164.}}}}

'''3.''' A bondman; a slave.
{{smaller block|<poem>Let such vile ''vassals'', borne to base vocation,
Drudge in the world, and for their living droyle,
Which have no wit to live withouten toyle.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', Mother Hub. Tale, l. 156.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Not ''vassals'' to be beat, nor pretty babes
To be dandled—no, but living wills.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Princess, iv.}}}}
{{smaller block|Men’s thoughts and opinions are in a great degree ''vassals'' of him who invents a new phrase or reapplies an old epithet.
{{right|''Lowell'', Among my Books, 2d ser., p. 326.}}}}

'''4.''' A low wretch.
{{smaller block|<poem>Obdurate ''vassals'' fell exploits effecting.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Lucrece, l. 429.}}}}

{{smaller|'''Great vassal''', under the feudal system, one who held lands directly from the sovereign without intermediary.—'''Rear vassal''', under the feudal system, a vassal of the second degree—that is, one who held land from a great vassal.}}

'''II.''' ''a.'' Servile; subservient.
{{smaller block|<poem>Silver golde in price doth follow,
Because from him, as Cynthia from Apollo,
She takes her light, & other mettals all
Are but his ''vassaile'' starres.</poem>
{{right|''Times’ Whistle'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 41.}}}}
{{smaller block|Thy proud heart’s slave and ''vassal'' wretch to be.
{{right|''Shak.'', Sonnets, cxli.}}}}

'''vassal''' (vas′ạl), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''vassaled'', ''vassalled'', ppr. ''vassaling'', ''vassalling''. [< ''vassal'', ''n.''] '''1.''' To subject to vassalage; enslave; treat as a vassal.
{{smaller block|How am I ''vassal’d'' then?
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Four Plays in One.}}}}
'''2.''' To command; rise over or above; dominate.
{{smaller block|<poem>Some proud hill, whose stately eminence
''Vassals'' the fruitfull vale’s circumference.</poem>
{{right|''W. Browne'', Britannia’s Pastorals, i. 4.}}}}

'''vassalage''' (vas′ạl-ạ̄j), ''n.'' [Formerly also ''vassallage'', ''vassellage''; < ME. ''vassalage'', ''vasselage'', < OF. ''vasselage'', ''vasalage'', ''vasselaige'', the service of a vassal, prowess, valor, also vassalage, F. ''vasselage'' = Pr. ''vassalatge'', ''vasselatge'' = Sp. ''vasallaje'' = Pg. ''vassallagem'' = It. ''vassallaggio'', vassalage; as ''vassal'' + ''-age''.] '''1.''' The state of being a vassal or feudatory; hence, the obligations of that state; the service required of a vassal.
{{smaller block|I protest I shall be proud to do you most obsequious ''vassalage''.
{{right|''Marston'', What you Will, ii. 1.}}}}
'''2.''' Servitude; dependence; subjection; slavery.
{{smaller block|Do you think that all they who live under a Kingly Government were so strangely in love with Slavery as, when they might be free, to chuse ''Vassalage?''
{{right|''Milton'', Ans. to Salmasius, vii.}}
<poem>But, slave to love, I must not disobey;
His service is the hardest ''vassalage''.</poem>
{{right|''Farquhar'', Love and a Bottle, iii. 1.}}}}
'''3.''' A territory held in vassalage; a fee or fief.

{{smaller block|And, which makes the more for Bellarmine, the French King was again ejected when our King submitted to the church, and the crown received under the sordid condition of a ''vassalage''. {{right|''Dryden'', Religio Laici, Pref.}}
The countship of Foix, with six territorial ''vassalages''. {{right|''Milman'', Latin Christianity, ix. 8.}}}}
'''4.''' Vassals or subjects collectively. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Like ''vassalage'' at unawares encountering
The eye of majesty. {{right|''Shak.'', T. and C., iii. 2. 40.}}</poem>}}
'''5†.''' Preëminence, as of one having vassals; hence, valor; prowess; courage.
{{smaller block|<poem>Al forgeten is his ''vasselage''.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Knight’s Tale, l. 2196.}}
Nor for thare plesand parsonage,
Nor for thare strenth nor ''vassalage''.
{{right|''Lauder'', Dewtie of Kyngis (E. E. T. S.), l. 284.}}
Catoun seyth, is none so gret encrese
Of worldly tresowre as for to lyve in pease
Which among vertues hath the ''vasselage''.
{{right|''Political Poems'', etc. (ed. Furnivall), p. 27.}}</poem>}}
{{smaller block|'''To do one vassalage''', to fulfil for one the duties of a vassal; render one the service of a vassal. ''Heywood'', Hierarchy of Angels, p. 477.}}

'''vassalate†''' (vas′al-āt), ''v. t.'' [< ''vassal'' + ''-ate''<sup>2</sup>.] To reduce to a state of vassalage or dependence; subordinate. ''Bp. Gauden'', Tears of the Church, p. 496. (''Davies.'')

'''vassalation†''' (vas-a̤-lā′sho̤n), ''n.'' [< ''vassalate'' + ''-ion.''] The state of being vassal or subject; vassalage.
{{smaller block|And this ''vassallation'' is a penalty set by the true Judge of all things upon our attempt to design of our own heads the forms of good and evil. {{right|''Montague'', Devoute Essays, xv. 2.}}}}

'''vassaless†''' (vas′al-es), ''n.'' [< ''vassal'' + ''-ess.''] A female vassal or dependent.
<poem>And be the vassall of his ''vassalesse''.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Spenser'', Daphnaïda, l. 181.}}}}

'''vassalry''' (vas′al-ri), ''n.'' [< ''vassal'' + -(''e'')''ry''.] The whole body of vassals; vassals collectively.

'''vast''' (vȧst), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [Early mod. E. ''vaste''; < OF. ''vaste'', F. ''vaste'' = Sp. Pg. It. ''vasto'', < L. ''vastus'', empty, unoccupied, desert, waste, desolate; hence, with ref. to extent as implied in emptiness, immense, enormous, huge, vast; akin to AS. ''wēste'', waste: see ''waste''<sup>1</sup>. Hence ''vastate'', ''devastate'', etc.] '''I.''' ''a.'' '''1†.''' Wide and vacant or unoccupied; waste; desolate; lonely.
{{smaller block|<poem>Of antres ''vast'' and deserts idle . . .
It was my hint to speak. ''Shak.'', Othello, i. 3. 140.</poem>}}
'''2.''' Being of great extent or size; very spacious or large; enormous; massive; immense.
{{smaller block|<poem>More devils than ''vast'' hell can hold.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', M. N. D., v. 1. 9.}}
Time with his ''vast'' Scythe mows down all Things, and Death sweeps away those Mowings. ''Howell'', Letters, ii. 44.
<poem>The mighty Rain
Holds the ''vast'' empire of the sky alone.</poem>
{{right|''Bryant'', Rain-Dream.}}
<poem>Black, thick, and ''vast'' arose that cloud.</poem>
{{right|''Whittier'', The Exiles.}}
<poem>Swells in the north ''vast'' Katahdin.</poem>
{{right|''Whittier'', Mogg Megone, ii.}}}}
'''3.''' Very great in quantity, number, or amount.
{{smaller block|The King’s Plate that is gathered in this Kingdom [Mexico], together with what belongs to the Merchants, amounts to a ''vast'' Summ. ''Dampier'', Voyages, II. ii. 125.
A ''vast'' number of chapels dressed out in all their finery of altar-pieces, embroidery, gilding, and marble.
{{right|''Gray'', Letters, I. 18.}}}}
<poem>An army of phantoms ''vast'' and wan
Beleaguer the human soul.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Longfellow'', The Beleaguered City.}}}}

'''4.''' Very great as to degree, intensity, difficulty of accomplishment, importance, etc.; mighty: used also in exaggerated colloquial speech, being much affected in the eighteenth century.
{{smaller block|’Tis a ''vast'' honour that is done me, gentlemen.
{{right|''Vanbrugh'', Æsop, v. i.}}}}
{{smaller block|Lady Stafford and Mrs. Pitt were in ''vast'' beauty.
{{right|''Walpole'', Letters, II. 153.}}}}
{{smaller block|The affairs of the general government, foreign and domestic, are ''vast'' and various and complicated.
{{right|''D. Webster'', Speech, Boston, June 5, 1828.}}}}
{{smaller|='''Syn. 2.''' Spacious.—'''3''' and '''4.''' Colossal, gigantic, prodigious, tremendous, stupendous.}}

'''II.''' ''n.'' '''1.''' A boundless waste or space; immensity.
{{smaller block|They have seemed to be together, though absent, shook hands, as over a ''vast'', and embraced, as it were from the ends of opposed winds.
{{right|''Shak.'', W. T., i. 1. 33.}}}}
{{smaller block|The ''vast'' of heaven.
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., vi. 203.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Swifter than thought the wheels instinctive fly,
Flame thro’ the ''vast'' of air, and reach the sky.</poem>
{{right|''Pope'', Iliad, viii. 544.}}}}
'''2.''' A great deal; a large quantity or number. [Local, Eng.]
{{smaller block|It were a ''vast'' o’ people went past th’ entry end.
{{right|''Mrs. Gaskell'', Sylvia’s Lovers, vii.}}}}
'''3.''' The darkness of night, in which the prospect is not bounded in by distinct objects: only in the following passage.<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
